extracted_by: hand, T-0258 piece 2 — the Democrat read, December 1833 (Vol. I Nos. 2-6)
note: Vol. I No. 2, 1833-12-03 — the second number ever printed in Chicago, and the first ordinary issue. Eight claims. THE TOWN IS ON PAGES 1 AND 3: page 1 column 1 carries the paper's own imprint and then the standing advertisement column, and page 3 columns 5 and 6 carry the school, the butcher, the prices current and the village ordinances; pages 2 and 4 are national reprint, Congressional matter and miscellany and carry no town claim. THIS ISSUE'S BOTTOM-OF-COLUMN OCR IS THE WORST IN THE MONTH — lines 92 to 134 of page 1 column 1 hold four advertisements and are barely English — so the two claims taken from that stretch (c002 Goss & Cobb, c003 W. Kimball) rest on their one legible line each and say so. THE DIALECT: a bare `SOURCE PDF PAGE 5` banner, which names the SCAN page and not the issue's (No. 1 occupies pages 1-4), so page numbers here are resolved ORDINALLY by the rule data/research/newspapers/README.md states. WHAT THIS ISSUE ADDS THAT NOTHING BEFORE IT HAD: the Chicago English & Classical Academy's address (c005) and the market square (c006). T-0258 PIECE 2 — DECEMBER 1833, Vol. I Nos. 2-6, five issues, read through. NO POST-OFFICE LETTER LIST STANDS ANYWHERE IN THE MONTH: all five transcriptions were swept for every form the Democrat uses elsewhere — 'list of letters', 'letters remaining', 'remaining in the post office', 'uncalled for', a signature ending 'P. M.' and the bare words 'post office' — for three hits, none of them a list (a Detroit post-office contract and a 'send by the Post-Office at our risk' line on 1833-12-10, and the President's message on the General Post Office Department on 1833-12-31). The epic's ruling 1 is therefore met by demonstrating absence, as T-0261 met it for the American and T-0308 for November; only four of T-0258's thirty issues carry a list and none of them is in December. THE MONTH'S STANDING ADVERTISEMENTS ARE CLAIMED ONCE, AT THEIR BEST-READ PRINTING, NOT FIVE TIMES. Sixteen cards run unchanged across two or more of these issues, and the OCR of each varies wildly from setting to setting; a claim is made in the issue where the line that carries the evidence is legible, and the other settings are named in its note as the cross-check. That is why the per-issue counts are uneven (8/12/7/7/7) and why a card that first appears in Vol. I No. 2 may be claimed from Vol. I No. 3. The alternative — one claim per printing — would have multiplied the same forty-one readings into about ninety and made the gazetteer's first_seen dates no better. THE ESTRAY NOTICES ARE QUARANTINED AND NOT CLAIMED, as T-0308 quarantined them: 'Taken Up' by Harry Boardman on the Du Page, by William See at Walker's Grove and by William Taylor in the county are Cook county filings attested by the Clerk of the Commissioners' Court, not Chicago matter, and the animals and appraisers in them belong to the county's prairie and not to the town. THE DEPOSIT IS ON `main` AND THIS BRANCH IS `dev`, so every quote here was machine-checked with `tools/compile_gazetteer.py --check --deposit <a read-only copy of the deposit from main>` before the PR was opened; on `dev` these claims are counted unresolved and reported, which is green (T-0275).

placement.anchor: the corner of Water and Franklin streets

claims.notes: THE SCHOOL GETS AN ADDRESS, AND THIS IS THE FIRST ISSUE THAT PRINTS IT. Vol. I No. 1 reported only that 'A school has recently been established in this village, By Mr. Sproat of Boston' (1833-11-26 c003) — no place, no name. Here it is the Chicago English & Classical Academy standing at the corner of Water and Franklin streets, under G. T. Sproat as preceptor, a fortnight later. 1834-01-07 c010 carries the same heading a month on, so the address is stable across the winter; this is its earliest printing. The corner is the JUNCTION and not a quadrant, and nothing here says whether the school occupies a building of its own or a room in one — the advertisement says only 'It has a room well adapted for the purpose' (1833-12-10, page 1 column 2), which if anything argues it is a room in another building.

placement.note: UNRESOLVED ANCHOR. This reconstruction holds no feature named "the market square"; the phrase is recorded as the paper prints it and mapped onto nothing.

claims.notes: THE MARKET SQUARE, NAMED AS A PLACE A BUILDING STANDS ON. This is the first mention in the corpus of a butcher's market ON the market square, and it is a placement in the town: a wholesale butcher's shop two miles out, and the retail market in Chicago on the square. The proprietor's name is the one thing this column will not give up — the signature line reads 'tela ed rial ok BR BUR,' and every candidate reading of it would be an invention, so NO NAME IS CLAIMED and the business is recorded unnamed. The hog count (four to five hundred in one week, corn-fed) is the strongest single figure this corpus holds on the scale of the town's provision trade in 1833.

claims.notes: BREWSTER, HOGAN & CO. CALLING IN THEIR ACCOUNTS. Claimed for the dateline and the firm rather than for the notice: 'Dec. 3, 1833' is this advertisement's own copy date, which is the day of the issue, so the firm is trading in Chicago on that day under that style. The body is recovered from the same notice set clean in 1833-12-10 (page 1 column 2, lines 225-234) and every supply is bracketed. The transcription DUPLICATES a line here — 'the proper o' and then 'he proper officer far collection' — and both copies are quoted as they stand and read once.

The reporter's name is garbled differently in every December setting — 'P,P. Pee' here, 'P. E. Pack' on 1833-12-10, 'P. I. Ped' on 1833-12-17 — and 1833-12-24 sets it clean as 'P. F.
